lines.text: Gold and emeralds, liberators and poets, war and a hard-won peace. This is the story of Colombia, from its ancient statue-makers to today.
High in the southern Andes, an ancient people carved great stone statues at San Agustin, guardians of their dead.
In the mountains of the Sierra Nevada, the Tairona built a city of stone terraces. Lost to the jungle, it was found again in 1972.
On the high plains, the Muisca offered gold to their gods in a lake, and gave rise to the legend of El Dorado.
Then the Spanish came. On the Caribbean they founded Cartagena, a walled port where the treasure fleets loaded silver and gold.
A few years later, they founded Bogota on the high plain of the Muisca, the future capital of New Granada.
In the valleys of Antioquia, Medellin grew up, a city that would know both terror and renewal.
In Venezuela, Simon Bolivar was born. He would lead the armies that freed much of South America from Spain.
In 1810, the people of New Granada declared their independence, and the long struggle for Colombia began.
Bolivar joined today's Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama into one great republic, Gran Colombia. Rivalries broke it apart within about a decade.
The decisive day came at Boyaca in 1819, where Bolivar's victory freed New Granada from Spanish rule.
But Liberals and Conservatives kept fighting. After the Thousand Days' War at the turn of the century, Panama broke away.
From the Caribbean town of Aracataca came Gabriel Garcia Marquez, whose One Hundred Years of Solitude made magic realism known worldwide.
In Bogota, the Gold Museum began to gather the treasures of the ancient peoples, tens of thousands of pieces of gold.
In 1948, the murder of the popular leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan set Bogota on fire with riots.
Pablo Escobar was born, the man who would build the Medellin drug cartel and hold a nation hostage.
The riots spread into La Violencia, ten years of political killing between Liberals and Conservatives across the countryside.
Juan Manuel Santos would one day be the president who made peace with the guerrillas.
Alvaro Uribe would be the president who fought them hard, from 2002 to 2010.
And Gustavo Petro, once a guerrilla himself, would become Colombia's first left-wing president.
In 1964 the FARC took up arms, beginning a guerrilla war against the state that would last more than fifty years.
In Barranquilla, Shakira was born, the singer who would carry Colombian music to the whole world.
In 1985 the volcano Nevado del Ruiz melted its ice, and mudflows buried the town of Armero in the night. The warnings came too late.
And in 2016, after half a century of war, Colombia signed a peace deal with the FARC.
From the gold of the Muisca to a fragile peace, Colombia keeps writing its own story.
